summary: This unit teaches you to manage workplace (industrial) relations in a Jamaican organisation: to explain the system, laws and bodies; to build good relations through policy, consultation and communication; to work with unions and collective agreements; to handle grievances and discipline fairly; to prepare, cost and conduct negotiations; to deal with disputes and industrial action; and to manage change and redundancy lawfully.

blocks.p: Workplace (industrial) relations is about the relationship between an employer and its workers, and between the employer and any union that represents them. Good relations mean fewer disputes, steadier output and a workplace where people trust that decisions are fair. This unit prepares managers and human resource staff to build good relations, to handle grievances and discipline fairly, to take part in collective bargaining, to deal with disputes and industrial action, and to manage restructuring and redundancy lawfully.
The unit is for supervisors, managers and human resource officers in private firms, hotels, factories, schools and public bodies in Jamaica.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it means in practice
rows: Name the parties, the main laws by purpose, and the roles of the Ministry of Labour and the Industrial Disputes Tribunal
Set a clear workplace relations policy, consult, communicate and monitor the climate
Understand recognition, bargaining units, delegates and collective agreements
Use the procedure, meet promptly and keep records
Investigate, tell the worker the allegation, hold a hearing, decide consistently and allow appeal
Prepare with a mandate and costings, bargain in good faith, record and implement agreements
Use conciliation and the Tribunal, and protect the business and relationships during action
Consult, use fair criteria, avoid unlawful reasons and pay what is due

blocks.note: Laws are explained here by their purpose, not by section numbers or penalties. When a real case arises, check the current law, the collective agreement, the company's policy and the Ministry of Labour's guidance, and take advice from your human resource or legal adviser.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: The industrial relations system in Jamaica

blocks.p: Industrial relations in Jamaica rests on three parties, often called **tripartite**:

head: Party
Role
rows: Run the business, set terms of work, bargain with unions, and belong to bodies such as employers' federations and trade associations
Workers have the right to join a union of their choice; unions represent members in bargaining, grievances and disputes, and are grouped in national union federations
Makes the laws, provides conciliation and advice through the Ministry of Labour, and runs the Industrial Disputes Tribunal

blocks.h: Main laws and bodies, by purpose

head: Law or body
What it is for
rows: Labour relations and industrial disputes law
Sets the framework for union recognition, collective bargaining, settling disputes, and the Industrial Disputes Tribunal; protects the right to organise
Practical guidance on good practice, including fair discipline, grievances and good-faith bargaining; breaches count as evidence in disputes
Notice, reasons for dismissal, redundancy procedure and payments
Maternity leave, equal pay, minimum wage, vacation, holidays, sexual harassment, disability and occupational safety and health
Offers advice, conciliation, and ministerial action such as ordering a poll on union recognition and referring a dispute to the Tribunal
Hears disputes referred by the Minister, including some dismissal cases, and makes awards

blocks.note: A manager must know the purpose of each law, the company's own policy and the collective agreement. If there is a conflict, the law prevails, then the agreement, then policy.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Workers have the **right to join a union** and to take part in its lawful activities. An employer must not threaten, bribe or punish a worker for joining or refusing to join a union.
A worker has a right to be dealt with fairly in discipline and dismissal.
A worker has protection against unlawful reasons for dismissal, such as pregnancy, union membership or activity, or discrimination.
An employer has the right to manage, to set reasonable rules and to expect work in return for pay, but it must act reasonably and keep to the law and to agreements.

blocks.h: Union recognition and the bargaining unit

blocks.p: A union's strength in a unit can be shown as a share: **members ÷ workers in the unit × 100**. If a union represents 300 of the 480 workers in a unit, its share is 62.5%. Where a courier company's 80 drivers are said to be mostly in a union, the company should acknowledge the letter, avoid any pressure on the drivers, check the facts and, if it disagrees, allow the Ministry's poll to settle it.

A union is **recognised** when an employer agrees (or is required) to bargain with it for a group of workers. That group is the **bargaining unit**: workers who share similar work, terms and interests, such as 'all production and packing workers'. If a union says it represents most of the workers in a unit and the employer disagrees, the usual way to settle it is **a poll of the workers, arranged by the Ministry of Labour**. The employer must not interfere with the poll.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Negotiation between an employer and a union about pay and terms of work
A written agreement between employer and union on pay and terms, binding on the parties and the workers in the unit
A worker elected by union members to represent them at the workplace
Deduction of union dues from pay, as agreed, and paid to the union
The union recognised to negotiate for a unit
A group of managers and worker representatives that discusses workplace matters

blocks.p: A collective agreement normally covers: the parties and the bargaining unit; pay rates and increases; hours and overtime; leave and holidays; allowances and benefits; the grievance and disciplinary procedures; arrangements for union delegates, time off and check-off; consultation; the length of the agreement and how it is reviewed. Management must know every term so it can apply the agreement fairly, and brief supervisors.

ul: Deal with the recognised union for matters in the agreement. Share the information needed for bargaining.
Allow union delegates reasonable time, as the agreement or code provides, to represent members.
Do not favour non-members or members, and do not use rewards or threats to influence membership.
Meet regularly, not only when there is a problem.

blocks.p: A written policy tells everyone how the organisation deals with people and how issues are raised and handled. It makes decisions predictable and lets staff know the rules. It should cover:

ul: the organisation's commitment to fair treatment and to the law;
how the organisation communicates and consults;
the grievance and disciplinary procedures, with time limits and rights of appeal and representation;
relations with unions and the JCC;
equal opportunity, harassment, and safety and health;
confidentiality and records;
who is responsible: the board, managers, supervisors and employees.

head: Who
Role
rows: Sets the policy, provides resources and models fair behaviour
Advises on law and agreement, trains managers, runs procedures, keeps records and manages relations with the union
Handles daily issues fairly before they grow; applies rules consistently; listens
Represents members and raises their concerns with managers
Follows the rules, raises concerns properly and does the job

blocks.p: Many disputes begin with rumours. Share information early and honestly, even when it is bad news. Use team briefings, notices, a JCC and regular meetings with union leaders. **Consultation** means asking for views before decisions are final and taking them seriously; it is different from simply announcing a decision.

blocks.note: A union delegate who hears rumours of a new shift system should be met promptly. Share what you can, say plainly what is not yet decided, and promise to consult before decisions are final.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A JCC's main purpose is to **discuss workplace matters and plans before decisions are taken**. It is not a place for bargaining pay (that is for the bargaining team) but it builds trust. Agree its terms of reference: members, how often it meets, agenda, minutes and how its advice is used.

head: Indicator
What a bad trend suggests
rows: Low morale, illness or poor management

blocks.p: **Rising absence, grievances and turnover together** are a strong sign that relations in a department are getting worse. Look for the cause, often supervision, workload or pay, and act before it becomes a dispute.

head: Point
Cooperative (partnership)
Adversarial (conflict)
rows: Both sides share interests in a successful business
Each side sees the other as an opponent
Held back as a bargaining weapon
Joint, through JCCs and early talks
Fewer disputes, higher trust and productivity; takes time to build
Short-term gains, more disputes and stoppages, lost trust

blocks.p: A company should aim for a **cooperative approach**, while keeping firm on what it cannot afford. Cooperation does not mean giving in; it means talking honestly and early.

blocks.h: A first-year plan when workers vote for a union

ol: Accept the result, and write to the union to say that the company will work with it as the law and the Ministry's process provide.
Meet the union officers early to agree how to work together: meetings, delegates' time off, check-off, information sharing.
Brief all supervisors on the law and the rights of workers and union; stop any pressure on membership.
Review the workplace relations policy and the grievance and disciplinary procedures with the union.
Prepare for the first collective agreement: facts, costings and a mandate.
Set up a JCC and regular team briefings.
Monitor absence, grievances and turnover; review progress after six and twelve months.

blocks.p: Trust grows when management **keeps its promises, shares information openly, treats people consistently and listens**. It is lost quickly by broken promises, favouritism and secrecy.

A **grievance** is a worker's complaint about the way she is treated, such as unfair overtime allocation, a supervisor's behaviour, or a breach of the agreement. A **dispute** is a wider disagreement, often between the union and the employer, over pay or terms. A grievance procedure aims to settle complaints early, at the lowest level, fairly and quickly.

flow: The worker raises the matter with her immediate supervisor, informally or in writing
If not settled in the time limit, she (with her union delegate if she wishes) refers it to the department head
If not settled, it goes to the human resource manager or a senior manager
If not settled, the union and management meet at the level set in the agreement
If still unsettled, it may be reported to the Ministry of Labour as a dispute

blocks.p: Track the system: if 21 of 30 grievances were settled at the first stage, that is 21 ÷ 30 × 100 = 70%. A high first-stage rate suggests supervisors are solving problems early.

ul: Each stage has a **time limit** (for example five working days) so that problems are dealt with before they grow.
The worker may be accompanied by a union delegate or a fellow worker.
Hear the worker promptly, listen without interrupting and ask questions to understand the facts.
Decide fairly, in writing, and give the right to go to the next stage.
Keep a record of each meeting and decision.

blocks.note: A supervisor who receives a formal grievance should meet the worker promptly, as the procedure says. Delay makes workers feel ignored and turns small complaints into disputes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A worker who feels she was unfairly passed over for overtime should use the **company's grievance procedure first**. If the matter involves a collective agreement point, the union can take it up. Posting the complaint on social media is not a stage of any procedure; it damages the employer and the worker, and can complicate settlement.

ol: Listen to the facts; do not defend the decision before hearing the worker.
Check the policy and the agreement.
Investigate: speak to others involved and check records.
Decide, explain the reasons and say what will be done.
Follow up to see that the remedy has happened and that the worker is not treated worse for complaining.

blocks.p: Discipline is how an employer deals with misconduct or poor behaviour. Fair discipline protects the workplace, and fair process protects the employer if a dismissal is challenged at the Tribunal.

ul: **Rules are known**: the standards and penalties are written and communicated.
**Investigate first**: collect facts, statements and records before deciding to hold a hearing.
**Tell the worker the allegation** in writing, with the evidence, and give time to prepare.
**Let the worker answer**: hold a hearing where she can respond, call witnesses and ask questions.
**Let the worker be accompanied** by a union delegate or fellow worker.
**An impartial decision-maker** who was not involved in the incident.
**Consistent penalties**: similar cases receive similar penalties. Unequal treatment makes a dismissal look unfair.
**A proportionate penalty** that takes into account the seriousness of the offence and the worker's record.
**Right of appeal** to a more senior manager.
**Written record** of every stage.

flow: An incident or report comes to management
Investigating officer collects statements, records and footage and reports the facts
If there is a case to answer, the worker is invited to a hearing in writing, with the allegation, evidence and her right to be accompanied
At the hearing, the allegation is explained, the worker answers, witnesses are heard and the hearing is recorded
The manager decides on the balance of probabilities and on the penalty, then confirms it in writing with reasons
The worker is told of her right to appeal, and any appeal is heard by someone more senior
Records are kept and the penalty is applied consistently

blocks.p: **Natural justice** is the name for the basic principles of fair procedure: the right to know the case against you and to answer it, and the right to a decision by someone who is unbiased. Every disciplinary process must follow them.

A disciplinary decision is based on the **balance of probabilities**: after a reasonable investigation, is it more likely than not that the worker did what is alleged? It is not necessary to prove it beyond all doubt, as in a criminal court, but the decision must rest on evidence, not suspicion.

Suspension during an investigation is not a penalty and should be used only when needed (for example, risk to evidence, to safety or to other workers). It should be on full pay as the rules provide, for as short a time as possible, and reviewed.

head: Level
Examples
Usual response
rows: Occasional lateness, small breach of procedure
Counselling, verbal warning, then written warning
Repeated breach after warning; unsafe act; neglect of duty
Written warning, final warning, or dismissal for repeated or very serious cases
Theft, fraud, violence, serious safety breach, being drunk on duty
May justify dismissal even for a first offence, after a fair process

blocks.p: Factors to consider: the seriousness; the worker's length of service and record; whether she was warned; how others in the same position were treated; any special circumstances; what the policy and agreement say.

blocks.note: Two cashiers who broke the same cash-handling rule must be treated alike unless there is a real difference between their cases. If one is warned and the other dismissed, the dismissal will look unfair.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Misconduct is a failure to follow rules. **Poor performance** is a failure to reach the standard. Handle poor performance by setting clear targets, giving training and support and a fair time to improve, then warnings if there is no improvement.

**Constructive dismissal** is when a worker resigns because the employer's serious breach of the contract (such as cutting pay without agreement, or serious unfair treatment) left her no real choice. The resignation is treated like a dismissal, so employers must not push people out by breaking their terms.

blocks.h: Unlawful and unfair reasons for dismissal

ul: Pregnancy and maternity.
Joining or taking part in lawful union activity.
Making a complaint or taking part in a proceeding.
Discrimination on unlawful grounds.
Refusing to do something that is unsafe or illegal.

blocks.p: A manager who suggests not renewing a worker's contract because she is pregnant should be told to refuse. It is unfair and may break employment law.

Keep careful records of grievance and disciplinary meetings: they show that a fair process was followed if the case is challenged. Keep details **confidential** to those who need to know. A supervisor should not tell the team why a colleague received a final warning. Records are personal data, so keep them secure and keep only what you need.

flow: Notice of the claim or review date of the agreement
Management and the union prepare separately
Exchange of the claim, information and costings
Talks: offers and counter-offers, trade-offs
Heads of agreement written and signed
The union takes it to members; management to the board if needed
Final agreement drawn up and signed
Briefing, payroll and records updated

ul: **Mandate**: agree with the board the highest offer and the terms the team may accept. The team may not go beyond its mandate.
**Facts**: the company's finances, the cost of living, productivity, pay for similar jobs at other firms in the area, the law and the agreement.
**The claim**: cost every item.
**Aims and limits**: opening position, target, walk-away point and trade-offs.
**Roles**: lead negotiator, costing officer, recorder, and an observer.
**The other side's interests**: why does the union want this?

blocks.p: Annual cost of a rise = employees × average monthly pay × 12 × percentage rise.

head: Example
Working
Result
rows: 80 workers, average J$70,000 a month; union claims 8%
Board mandate of 5% for the same group
Two-year deal: 4% then 3%, each on the pay at the time, for a worker on J$70,000
A stoppage of 4 days where output is 500 units a day, contribution J$2,000 a unit
Monthly payroll J$6,000,000 and a rise of 4% for everyone
The board limits extra pay to J$5,760,000 a year; 120 workers on J$80,000 a month
The limit allows a rise of 5%
Union claims 9%, management offers 3%, and they settle halfway

blocks.note: Do not add percentages together for a two-year deal. 4% then 3% is not 7%, because the second rise is on the higher pay. Always remember that payroll contributions and overtime rise with pay, so the full cost is above the basic pay change.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **position** is what a side demands ('12%'). An **interest** is why ('workers worry about the cost of travelling home after late shifts'). Negotiators who ask questions can find interests and trade-offs that satisfy both sides, such as a transport allowance and a smaller general increase, or a job-security promise, training or better shift arrangements.

ul: Meet regularly and attend on time.
Share the information needed for talks.
Listen and make real proposals, not only refusals.
Do not make threats, go over the union's head to members, or break agreed confidentiality.
Aim for agreement.
Before leaving the room, **write the main terms and have the lead speakers sign them** as heads of agreement.
If the agreed terms go beyond the mandate, the management team signs only 'subject to board approval', or goes back to the board first.
Union leaders usually take the terms to members for approval.
Then the full agreement is drawn up, and the HR manager briefs supervisors and updates payroll, policies and records.

blocks.p: If talks fail, record the issues in dispute, with each side's final position, for conciliation.

flow: Grievance or bargaining talks at the workplace
If no settlement, a party reports the dispute to the Ministry of Labour
Ministry conciliation officers help the parties talk and reach their own agreement
If conciliation fails, the Minister may refer the dispute to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal
The Tribunal hears both sides and makes an award
The award is binding on the parties; both implement it

head: Body
What it does
rows: Helps the two sides talk and reach their own agreement; the officer does not decide
Hears disputes referred to it and makes awards that are binding on the parties; it can also hear cases of dismissal that are referred to it

blocks.p: If a dispute about a dismissal goes to the Tribunal, the employer needs **records that show the reasons for the dismissal and the fair process followed**: investigation notes, hearing notes, warnings, letters and evidence of consistency. Good records often decide the case.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Workers stop work together in a dispute
Workers stay at their posts but deliberately work more slowly
Workers do exactly what their job descriptions and rules require, and nothing more, which slows work
Many workers report sick on the same day as industrial action
Standing at the workplace entrance to publicise a dispute
Staying in the workplace and refusing to leave
A stoppage in support of another group's dispute, not the strikers' own
The employer closes the workplace or keeps workers out until they accept its terms

blocks.p: The law restricts industrial action. In particular, industrial action in **essential services** (for example, health services, water, electricity and fire services) is controlled by special rules, and action over a matter that has been referred to the Tribunal is generally not allowed. Because the details are legal, a manager should take advice at the time.

blocks.h: What management does during industrial action

ol: Stay calm and keep talking with the union. Ask what the workers want and what would end the action.
Check the legal position and tell the union that you will follow it.
Protect safety, assets and people who want to work; do not allow intimidation from any side.
Run a contingency plan for customers: warn them early and honestly of delays.
Do not victimise or punish workers for lawful action, and treat everyone equally afterwards.
Keep records of lost output, costs and events.
Use the Ministry's conciliation if direct talks fail.

blocks.p: The cost of a stoppage is lost output (the contribution that would have been earned), plus lost customers, penalties and the cost of rebuilding relations. A short, honest talk early is nearly always cheaper than days of stoppage.

The employer cannot normally change a worker's terms (hours, pay, place of work) alone. If management wants to change them, for example a move from a five-day to a six-day week, it should **consult the workers and their union and seek agreement first**, explain the reason, listen to the effects on people (child care, transport, second jobs), consider alternatives and give enough notice. A change forced through without agreement may break the contract and the collective agreement and can lead to a dispute.
A redundancy occurs when a post is no longer needed, for example because a contract ended, a unit closed or technology changed. It is about the job, not the person.

flow: Confirm the business reason and the numbers
Look for ways to avoid or reduce redundancies
Consult the union and workers early, and notify the Ministry of Labour and union as the law requires
Agree fair, objective selection criteria
Apply the criteria and consider redeployment
Tell each affected person privately and give the reasons
Pay everything due and support those leaving

head: Ways to avoid or reduce redundancy
Notes
rows: Do not fill posts that become vacant
Staff who wish to leave volunteer

ul: **Selection criteria** must be fair, objective, job-related and applied to everyone in the affected group. Never select because of union membership, pregnancy, gender, age or a complaint.
**Tell affected staff individually and in private** before any general announcement.
**Final pay**: notice or pay in lieu, any accrued vacation pay, any redundancy payment due by law, and the agreed documents.
Support those leaving (reference letters, time to look for jobs, counselling), and support those who stay: they may be anxious, and workloads may rise.

blocks.note: Staff who remain after redundancies often worry about their own jobs. Tell them the plan openly, review workloads and offer support.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Pregnancy**: a worker cannot be dismissed or refused a renewal because of pregnancy. Know the maternity leave rights.
**Harassment and discrimination**: investigate every complaint seriously and fairly; protect the complainant from retaliation.

**Safety**: if workers refuse to use a machine they believe is unsafe and the union backs them, **stop the machine and have it checked with the workers**. Do not threaten discipline for a genuine safety concern.

blocks.p: Keep a file for each case and agreement. Share information only with those who need it, keep records secure and follow the data protection law.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, many large employers have a recognised union, but many small ones do not. Your workplace relations policy should work for both: fair, written and well communicated.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: name the three parties and explain the role of the Ministry of Labour and the Industrial Disputes Tribunal.
explain union recognition, a bargaining unit, a collective agreement and the role of a union delegate.
write the main parts of a workplace relations policy and describe the line manager's role.
describe a grievance procedure and handle a formal grievance promptly.
run a fair disciplinary process: investigate, tell the worker the allegation, hold a hearing, decide consistently and allow appeal.
explain the balance of probabilities, suspension and the choice of penalty.
prepare for wage talks with a mandate, facts and costings, and cost a claim and a two-year deal correctly.
separate positions from interests and bargain in good faith.
record an agreement and implement it.
describe conciliation and the Tribunal and the different forms of industrial action.
respond to industrial action calmly, lawfully and with a contingency plan.
consult on changes and manage redundancy with fair criteria, private notice and correct final pay.

terms: A worker's complaint about her treatment.
A wider disagreement, often between a union and an employer.
The group of workers a union is recognised to bargain for.
A written agreement between employer and union on pay and terms.
A worker elected to represent union members at work.
The limits on what the negotiating team may offer or accept.
A signed summary of the main terms reached in talks.
Help from the Ministry of Labour so the sides reach their own agreement.
The body that hears referred disputes and makes binding awards.
Doing only what the job description and rules require.
The employer shuts out workers until they accept its terms.
Loss of a job because the post is no longer needed.
More likely than not, the standard for disciplinary decisions.

c1.title: A union claims recognition at an agro-processing factory
c1.text: An agro-processing factory in Westmoreland employs 140 people: 95 in production and packing, 25 in the warehouse and drivers' pool, and 20 in the office and management grades. A union writes to the human resource manager, Mr Dunn, saying that most of the production and packing workers have signed up and asking to bargain for them. Mr Dunn is unsure whether the signatures are real. One supervisor has told workers that anyone who signs will 'be remembered at promotion time'. A union delegate has asked for an hour of work time to help a member with a grievance.

c2.title: A market inspector is accused of keeping vendors' fees
c2.text: At a municipal corporation in Mandeville, vendors complain that market inspector Neville Gayle collected stall fees on several days without giving receipts. Gayle has served for 15 years with a clean record. The manager, Ms Bailey, must decide how to proceed. A union delegate has offered to accompany Gayle. Two years ago another inspector, found to have kept fees, was dismissed after a hearing.

c3.title: Wage talks at a furniture factory
c3.text: A furniture factory in St Andrew has 80 workers in the bargaining unit, with average pay of J$70,000 a month. The union claims an 8% rise. The board has told management it may agree to up to 5% for the first year. In the first round of talks, the union leader mentions that workers are really worried about job security because the factory has bought new cutting machines. Late one evening the team and the union reach a 6% heads of agreement.

c4.title: A dispute at a hotel laundry
c4.text: A laundry in Montego Bay washes linen for several hotels. Management wants to change from three shifts to two. The union opposes it. Direct talks have failed. The workers have begun to work at about half pace while staying at their machines, and the hotels are asking about delays. The manager wants to protect the contracts and the relationship with the workers.

c5.title: Restructuring at an insurance back office
c5.text: An insurance company in Kingston is closing its paper-claims unit and has identified 12 posts as redundant, out of 30 staff in the unit. The unit includes Mrs Palmer, who is expecting a baby, and a union delegate. The remaining staff will move their start time from 8:30 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Staff are anxious, and rumours say that the whole branch will close.

questions.q: Mr Dunn receives the union's letter. What is the best first response?
o: Ignore it until the union takes the matter to the Ministry of Labour
Ask the union for the names of its members so that managers can speak to them
Acknowledge it, check the facts and let the Ministry's poll settle any dispute
Reply that the company will deal only with its individual workers directly
questions.why: A recognition claim must be taken seriously. The employer should respond promptly and, where the claim is disputed, allow the process led by the Ministry of Labour to settle it, without interfering.

questions.q: Which group is most reasonable as a bargaining unit for the union's claim?
o: All production and packing workers, who share similar work and terms
Only those workers who have signed the union's membership forms so far
All 140 employees, including the office and management grades
The warehouse staff and drivers together with the department managers
questions.why: A bargaining unit is a group with similar work, terms and interests. Managers have different interests from production workers, and a group chosen by who has signed is not a proper unit.

questions.q: A delegate asks for an hour of work time to help a member with a grievance. What should Mr Dunn do?
o: Refuse, because union business should be done in the worker's own time
Allow it, but deduct the hour from the delegate's pay at month end
Allow it only if the grievance is about pay or overtime for the member
Allow reasonable time, as the agreement provides, and ask for notice
questions.why: A delegate needs reasonable time off to represent members. Good practice is to allow it, with notice to the supervisor so that work can be covered.

questions.q: What should Mr Dunn do about the supervisor who spoke about promotion?
o: Take no action, because the supervisor only gave a personal opinion
Stop the supervisor and remind all supervisors that workers may choose
Ask the supervisor to say the same thing to those who refuse to sign
Warn the union to stop recruiting for members during working hours
questions.why: Workers are entitled to join a union without threats or promised rewards. A manager who allows pressure risks a dispute and may breach the law.

questions.q: Ms Bailey is told that evidence may be changed if Gayle stays at the market. What is her best action?
o: Dismiss him at once, since several vendors have made a complaint
Consider a short suspension on full pay, then review it
Leave him in post, since suspension is in itself a penalty
Move him to another market without telling him the reason why
questions.why: Suspension is not a penalty. It may be used briefly, on full pay, when needed to protect evidence or people, and it should be reviewed. Dismissal before a hearing would be unfair.

questions.q: What should the invitation to the disciplinary hearing contain?
o: A statement that he has been found guilty, with the date of the hearing set
Only the date and time, so that he cannot prepare an excuse in advance
The allegation, with the vendors' names left out and no evidence attached to it
The allegation in writing, the evidence, the date and his right to be accompanied
questions.why: The worker must know the case against him and have time to prepare. Telling him the allegation, the evidence and his right to representation is part of a fair hearing.

questions.q: At the hearing, how sure must Ms Bailey be before she decides that the allegation is proved?
o: It must be more likely than not, based on the evidence
Beyond all reasonable doubt, as in a criminal trial in court
It is enough that several of the vendors dislike him
She may decide on her own opinion of his character and attitude
questions.why: In disciplinary matters the test is the balance of probabilities, after a reasonable investigation. The decision must rest on evidence, but proof beyond all doubt is not required.

questions.q: The allegation is proved. Which factors should Ms Bailey weigh in choosing the penalty?
o: Only his 15 years of service, since he has been a loyal employee
Only the previous dismissal, since the same penalty must always be given
The seriousness, his record, the policy, and how others were treated
Mainly the cost to the corporation of hiring and training a replacement
questions.why: A proportionate and consistent penalty weighs seriousness, the worker's record, the policy and how similar cases were treated. No single factor decides it.

questions.q: The union's claim of 8% is above the board's limit of 5%. By how much do the two differ in cost over a year?
questions.why: The yearly pay bill is 80 × J$70,000 × 12 = J$67,200,000. A rise of 8% costs J$5,376,000 and 5% costs J$3,360,000. The difference is J$2,016,000.

questions.q: By how much would the 6% heads of agreement exceed the board's 5% limit in yearly cost?
questions.why: 6% of J$67,200,000 is J$4,032,000 and 5% is J$3,360,000. The agreement goes J$672,000 a year over the board's limit, so the board must approve it.

questions.q: The union leader says workers are worried about job security. What should the lead negotiator do?
o: Ignore this and hold to the 5% mandate throughout all of the talks
Offer the full 8% so that all of the workers' worries are resolved at once
Tell the union that the new machines are not a topic for the talks
Explore a job-security promise and retraining, with a smaller rise
questions.why: Asking about interests reveals what workers really need. A job-security commitment or training may satisfy the union at a lower cost than a larger rise.

questions.q: The late-night heads of agreement is 6%, but the board's limit is 5%. What should the lead negotiator have done?
o: Sign without any condition, since the talks were hard won by both teams
Sign only subject to board approval, or go back to the board first
Sign and then tell the board that it now has no real choice but to agree
Refuse to sign any agreement until the union members have voted on it
questions.why: A negotiating team must stay within its mandate. If it wants to go beyond it, the terms must be made subject to the board's approval.

questions.q: Conciliation has failed. What may the Minister of Labour do next?
o: Order the workers back to work on the old pattern of shifts
Refer the dispute to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal
Decide the new shift pattern personally for the laundry
Close the laundry until the workers have agreed to two shifts
questions.why: If conciliation does not settle a dispute, the Minister may refer it to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal, which hears both sides and makes an award.

questions.q: The workers stay at their machines but work at about half pace. What is this called?
o: A lockout
A sick-out
A sit-in
A go-slow
questions.why: A go-slow is a deliberate reduction in the pace of work by workers who remain at their posts. A work-to-rule is different: it is a strict following of the rules.

questions.q: What is the best first priority for the laundry manager now?
o: Keep talking with the union and warn the hotels honestly of delays
Dismiss the slowest workers to frighten all of the others
Close the laundry and lock the workers out until they accept two shifts
Say nothing to the hotels so as not to cause them any worry
questions.why: Talking is the quickest route to an end of the action. Hotels should be told early so that they can plan; hiding delays loses trust and contracts.

questions.q: Once the dispute is before the Tribunal, what is the usual position on industrial action over that matter?
o: Either side may take any action it wishes, since the Tribunal is so slow
Only the employer may act, since it owns the laundry business
The parties should not take industrial action over it
Industrial action is needed to show that the dispute is a serious one
questions.why: A matter referred to the Tribunal is generally to be settled by its award, and industrial action over it is not usually permitted. The parties should check the legal position.

questions.q: How should the company choose which of the 12 people from the 30 will go?
o: Choose the staff who have made the most complaints to management
Select by the order in which the staff were hired, newest first, always
Agree objective, job-related criteria and apply them to all in the unit
Let each supervisor name the people whom he finds hardest to manage
questions.why: Selection must be fair and consistent. Criteria agreed in advance and applied to everyone avoid unlawful reasons such as union activity or pregnancy.

questions.q: How should the 12 selected staff be told?
o: Individually and in private, with their entitlements explained
In a general announcement made to everyone at the staff meeting
By a notice on the board in the staff canteen on the Friday
By a text message sent to each person at the end of the day
questions.why: A person losing a job should hear it first, privately and with the reasons, not from a notice or a rumour. Treating people with dignity also protects the company.

questions.q: What should be included in the final pay of those made redundant?
o: Only the pay for the days worked in the final month of employment
Only a redundancy payment, since notice is not owed in a redundancy
The final pay and a bonus that the manager may choose to give them
Notice or pay in lieu, accrued vacation pay and any redundancy payment due
questions.why: Workers made redundant are entitled to notice (or pay instead), accrued leave pay, and any redundancy payment due. Underpaying can lead to a claim.

questions.q: The remaining staff are anxious and working longer. What is the best response?
o: Tell them to be thankful that they still have a job to go to
Explain the plans openly, review workloads and offer support
Say nothing at all until the restructuring has been finished
Move the earlier start time to 7:30 to make up for lost output
questions.why: Staff who remain after redundancies need honest information and a manageable workload. Silence feeds rumours and hurts morale and output.
